summary: Page 14, Saddle River section, retrospective feature 'Newspaper of days ago remembered' by Tom Brady profiles Alfred P. Smith, a disabled Black man born in Saddle River in 1832 who single-handedly wrote, edited, printed, translated, and distributed the borough's only commercial newspaper, The Landscape (originally 'A.P. Smith's Paper'), from May 1881 to July 1901, when he died and the paper ceased. Smith started a job-printing business in 1876, used the paper to advertise it, covered local and national news, published poetry (including Edgar Allan Poe and his own German translations), spoke out against racism (citing Sen. Sumner's 'Barbarism of Slavery' speech), and predicted Bergen County's suburban growth. Article draws on David Steven Cohen's piece 'Alfred P. Smith: Bergen County's Latter-Day Ben Franklin' and thanks the Saddle River Landmarks Commission. Includes a photo portrait of Alfred P. Smith. Adjacent 'Lawmakers' items cover unrelated state pilot mail-claim and higher-education award news.

incidents.what: Alfred P. Smith started a job-printing business after his father died
Smith printed and distributed his newspaper (The Landscape, originally A.P. Smith's Paper) from a house on East Allendale Road; ceased publishing when he died in July 1901
Smith editorialized against racism, referencing Senator Sumner's 'Barbarism of Slavery' speech, writing that daily 'barbarism... would disgrace a nation of savages' still remained
Smith advocated paving Saddle River's roads; the paving vote was carried and $2,000 appropriated for the work; Smith also predicted Bergen County suburban growth

connections: Alfred P. Smith and his paper The Landscape/A.P. Smith's Paper (Saddle River, 1881-1901) are themselves a significant early NJ Black-press subject for the project; article also references the Hackensack Republican and Paterson Guardian, where Smith worked/contributed
